subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: HIV cannot replicate without a host cell because it:
options: Lacks the enzymes and ribosomes needed for protein synthesis and energy release
Is too small to contain genetic material
questions.explain: As a virus, HIV has no metabolic machinery of its own and must use the host cell's enzymes and ribosomes to replicate.

questions.q: In a pregnancy test, monoclonal antibodies are used to:
options: Bind specifically to the hCG hormone, giving a coloured line when present
questions.explain: Mobile antibodies bind hCG and are then trapped by immobilised antibodies in the test window, producing a visible coloured line.

questions.q: Which type of white blood cell is a non-specific phagocyte that engulfs pathogens?
questions.explain: Neutrophils are phagocytes that engulf and digest pathogens non-specifically as part of the innate immune response.

questions.q: Antibodies passed from mother to baby in breast milk give the baby:
questions.explain: The antibodies are received naturally (via milk/placenta) and the baby does not make them itself, so it is natural passive immunity.

questions.q: HIV is described as a retrovirus because it:
options: Contains RNA and uses reverse transcriptase to make DNA inside the host cell
questions.explain: HIV carries RNA and the enzyme reverse transcriptase, which produces DNA from the viral RNA so it can integrate into the host genome.

questions.q: Agglutination by antibodies helps destroy pathogens because:
options: It marks the antibody for destruction
It directly lyses the bacterial cell wall
It neutralises bacterial toxins by hydrolysis
Each antibody has two binding sites, so it clumps pathogens together, making them easier for phagocytes to engulf
questions.explain: With two binding sites an antibody can link several pathogens into clumps that phagocytes engulf more efficiently.

questions.q: Self-antigens normally do not trigger an immune response because:
options: Lymphocytes that would respond to the body's own antigens are destroyed or suppressed during development
They are too small to be detected
questions.explain: During development, lymphocytes complementary to self-antigens undergo clonal deletion or suppression, preventing autoimmune attack.

questions.q: Bacteria and viruses are examples of pathogens. A key difference relevant to immunity is that viruses:
options: Can only reproduce inside a host cell using its machinery
questions.explain: Viruses are intracellular parasites that hijack host-cell machinery to replicate, which is why they evade antibiotics.

questions.q: An antibody is a glycoprotein with a quaternary structure made up of:
options: Two heavy and two light polypeptide chains held by disulfide bonds
One heavy and three light chains
questions.explain: Each antibody consists of two identical heavy and two identical light chains linked by disulfide bridges, forming a Y-shaped molecule.

questions.q: An antibody molecule's specificity for a particular antigen is determined by:
options: The variable region, which forms the antigen-binding site
The disulfide bridges holding the chains together
The constant region of the heavy chains
The hinge region between the chains
questions.explain: The variable regions of the heavy and light chains form a binding site whose shape is complementary to a specific antigen.

questions.q: In cancer treatment, monoclonal antibodies can be used for 'targeted' drug delivery because they:
options: Bind specifically to antigens on cancer cells, carrying an attached drug only to those cells
Convert cancer cells back to normal
questions.explain: Antibodies specific to tumour antigens deliver a cytotoxic drug directly to cancer cells, reducing harm to healthy tissue.

questions.q: In the cell-mediated response, T-helper cells are activated when they:
options: Bind to antigens presented on the surface of an antigen-presenting cell
Bind directly to free antigens in the blood
questions.explain: T-helper cells have receptors complementary to antigens displayed by antigen-presenting cells, and this binding activates them.

questions.q: The ELISA test uses antibodies linked to an enzyme to:
options: Vaccinate a patient against a disease
Detect the presence of a specific antigen or antibody by producing a colour change
Destroy a pathogen in a sample
questions.explain: In an ELISA, an enzyme-linked antibody binds its target and the enzyme then catalyses a colour change, revealing presence and amount.

questions.q: When a B-cell is activated and divides, the process that produces many identical cells is called:
questions.explain: The selected B-cell divides by mitosis to form a clone of identical cells, some becoming plasma cells and others memory cells.

questions.q: An antigen is best defined as:
options: A molecule (usually protein) that is recognised as foreign and triggers an immune response
An antibody produced by plasma cells
A protein that always causes disease
questions.explain: Antigens are molecules, often surface proteins, identified as non-self and capable of stimulating an immune response.

questions.q: Recovering from chickenpox and becoming immune to it is an example of:
questions.explain: The body makes its own antibodies and memory cells in response to a natural infection, giving natural active immunity.

questions.q: After engulfing a pathogen, a macrophage often becomes an antigen-presenting cell. This means it:
options: Destroys all lymphocytes that bind to it
Displays the pathogen's antigens on its surface to activate lymphocytes
Stores the antigens permanently inside vesicles
questions.explain: By presenting antigens on its surface, the macrophage activates specific T-helper cells, linking innate and adaptive immunity.

questions.q: Why does an untreated HIV infection eventually leave a person vulnerable to opportunistic infections?
options: The falling number of T-helper cells weakens both humoral and cell-mediated responses
HIV destroys the bone marrow completely
questions.explain: As HIV depletes T-helper cells, the immune system can no longer coordinate effective responses, so normally harmless microbes cause disease.

questions.q: Activated T-helper cells assist the humoral response chiefly by:
options: Producing large amounts of antibody themselves
Releasing cytokines that stimulate B-cells and phagocytes
questions.explain: T-helper cells secrete cytokines (interleukins) that promote clonal expansion of B-cells and increase phagocytic activity.

questions.q: Some antibodies act as antitoxins. This means they:
options: Bind to and neutralise toxins released by pathogens
questions.explain: Antitoxins bind specifically to toxin molecules, neutralising them so they can no longer harm the body's cells.

questions.q: During phagocytosis of a pathogen, the engulfed microbe is destroyed when:
options: A phagosome fuses with a lysosome and lysozymes hydrolyse the pathogen
Antibodies are released into the cytoplasm
questions.explain: The pathogen is enclosed in a phagosome which fuses with a lysosome; lytic enzymes (lysozymes) then digest it.

questions.q: Herd immunity protects unvaccinated individuals because:
options: A high proportion of immune people reduces the chance of an unvaccinated person meeting an infected person
Antibodies are passed between people on contact
The pathogen mutates to become harmless
Vaccines spread immunity through the air
questions.explain: When enough of the population is immune, transmission is interrupted, so susceptible individuals are unlikely to encounter the pathogen.

questions.q: The clonal selection and activation of a specific B-cell typically requires:
options: Antigen binding plus stimulation by an activated T-helper cell releasing cytokines
Only the antigen binding to the B-cell receptor
questions.explain: Most B-cells require both antigen binding and signals (cytokines) from T-helper cells to divide and differentiate.

questions.q: In the cell-mediated response, cytotoxic (killer) T-cells destroy infected body cells by:
options: Releasing perforin, which makes holes in the cell membrane so the cell dies
questions.explain: Cytotoxic T-cells release perforin that perforates the membrane of infected cells, causing them to die before the pathogen can multiply.

questions.q: Antigenic variation makes some pathogens (e.g. influenza virus) hard to combat because:
options: They cannot be engulfed by phagocytes
They reproduce too slowly for memory cells to form
They destroy all the host's T-cells
They change their surface antigens, so memory cells from previous infections no longer recognise them
questions.explain: Frequent changes to surface antigens mean existing memory cells are no longer complementary, so a new primary response is needed each time.

questions.q: Receiving an injection of antibodies (e.g. anti-tetanus serum) provides:
questions.explain: Ready-made antibodies are introduced artificially without the body making its own, giving immediate but short-lived (passive) protection.

questions.q: The secondary immune response is faster and stronger than the primary because:
options: Antigens are weaker on second exposure
Memory cells rapidly divide and differentiate into plasma cells, producing antibodies quickly
questions.explain: Memory cells formed during the primary response allow a rapid proliferation of plasma cells and a higher, quicker antibody output.

questions.q: For herd immunity to interrupt transmission of a pathogen, the proportion of the population that must be immune depends mainly on:
options: How easily the pathogen spreads from person to person
The age of the youngest individual
The colour of the vaccine vial
questions.explain: More infectious pathogens require a higher proportion of immune individuals to break chains of transmission and protect the susceptible.

questions.q: Plasma cells differ from memory cells in that plasma cells:
options: Secrete large quantities of antibody but are short-lived
Divide rapidly on a second exposure
Remain in the blood for years
questions.explain: Plasma cells are antibody factories that live only a few days, whereas memory cells persist to give rapid future responses.

questions.q: A vaccine typically contains antigens that produce long-lasting immunity by:
options: Stimulating the body to make memory cells without causing the disease
questions.explain: Vaccines present harmless antigens that trigger a primary response and memory-cell formation, so future exposure is met rapidly.
